```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2movies)

clean_movies <- read_rds("clean_movies.rds")
```

# Linear regression

## Exploring single linear regression per interesting variable

1.  Year

2.  Genre

3.  Length

4.  Number of votes

## 1. Year

To investigate the correlation between the year of release of a movie
and the rate it received from users, we fit a linear model with year as
the predictor variable.

```{r}
model_year <- lm(mean_rating ~ year, data=clean_movies)
summary(model_year)

plot_lm_year <- model_year %>% 
  {par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(.)}
```

Although the p-value for the slope is significant (given an alpha =
0.001), the R^2^ value is low (0.09117), indicating that year of release
cannot predict rating through a linear model.

## 2. Genre

## 3. Length

## 4. Votes

We want to investigate whether the total number of votes can predict the
average rating of a movie. We do this by fitting a linear model to the
data using votes as a predictor of rating.

```{r}
fit_votes <- lm(rating ~ 1 + votes, data = clean_movies) 

summary(fit_votes)
```

# Visualise diagnostic plots of the linear model in one figure. These assess the criteria of: linearity, homoscedasticity, normality, and absence of outliers

```{r}
plot_lm_votes <- fit_votes %>% 
  {par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(.)}
```

Although the slope shows a low p-value, the adjusted R^2^ is low
(0.03139). The diagnostic plots indicate that the data may be not
linearly distributed or homoscedatic. We can try to fit a better model
using a log transformation.

```{r}
fit_votes_log <- 
  lm(rating ~ 1 + log(votes), 
     data = clean_movies) 

summary(fit_votes_log)

# Compare the adjusted R^2 of both models
summary(fit_votes_log)$adj.r.squared - 
  summary(fit_votes)$adj.r.squared   #log-transformed is higher

# Calculate Akaike's ‘An Information Criterion’ for both models
AIC(fit_votes, fit_votes_log) 
```

When we log-transform the votes variable, we obtain a slightly higher
adjusted R^2^ (0.04227) and the model is better !!worse because it is
higher!! according to the AIC metric. Even if it remains weak, the
correlation between amount of votes and rating is better explained by
this second model.

We can visualize the two predicted fit lines on the data in a scatter
plot of average rating against number of votes. Here, the votes are
colored by the percentage of users who awarded a 10/10 rate.

```{r}

votes_rating_plot <- ggplot(
  clean_movies, 
      aes(votes, rating)) +
      geom_point(aes(color = r10)) +
  labs(dictionary = c(
    votes = "Total user votes",
    rating = "Average rating /10",
    r10 = "Percentage of 10/10 votes")) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ 1 + x, 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "orange3", 
              linetype = 1) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ 1 + log(x), 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "red3", 
              linetype = 1) + 
  scale_color_viridis_c()

print(votes_rating_plot)
```
